questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In Group 15 of the periodic table, the stability of the $+5$ oxidation state decreases down the group from phosphorus to bismuth, whereas the stability of the $+3$ oxidation state progressively increases. Which of the following fundamental electronic factors is primarily responsible for this periodic trend?
options: A) Reluctance of the valence shell $ns^2$ electrons to participate in chemical bonding due to poor shielding by intervening $d$ and $f$ orbitals (inert pair effect)
B) Progressive increase in effective nuclear charge causing contraction of the valence $np$ subshell only
C) Decrease in electronegativity making the central atom incapable of forming covalent bonds with electronegative ligands
D) Increase in atomic volume leading to preferred delocalization of $d$ electrons into antibonding orbitals
questions.explanation:
Step 1: The valence shell electronic configuration of Group 15 elements is $ns^2 np^3$.
Step 2: Descending the group from nitrogen to bismuth, intervening filled $d$ and $f$ subshells are introduced. Because $d$ and $f$ electrons have poor screening (shielding) capacity, the effective nuclear charge felt by the outermost $ns^2$ electrons increases considerably.
Step 3: Consequently, the outer $ns^2$ pair of electrons becomes tightly held by the nucleus and remains inert (non-bonding), known as the inert pair effect. Hence, only the three $np$ electrons readily participate in bonding, making the $+3$ oxidation state increasingly stable down the group, while the $+5$ state becomes unstable and strongly oxidizing (for example, $\text{Bi(V)}$ is a powerful oxidizing agent).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Electronegativity decrease does not selectively destabilize $+5$ relative to $+3$; inner electron shielding of $s$-electrons rather than $np$-only contraction is the root cause; and Group 15 elements do not possess valence $d$-electron delocalization into antibonding orbitals in their elemental ground states.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Consider the hydrides of Group 15 elements: $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{PH}_3$, $\text{AsH}_3$, and $\text{SbH}_3$. The experimental $\text{H}-\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond angles decrease in the order $\text{NH}_3 (107.8^\circ) > \text{PH}_3 (93.6^\circ) > \text{AsH}_3 (91.8^\circ) > \text{SbH}_3 (91.3^\circ)$. Which of the following rationales accurately explains this continuous decrease?
options: A) Increasing atomic size increases lone pair-bond pair repulsion, forcing bond pairs closer into an $sp$ hybridization
B) Decreasing electronegativity of the central atom leads to greater spread of bond pair electrons away from the nucleus, decreasing bond pair-bond pair repulsion
C) Increasing bond length enhances steric crowding around the central atom, compelling compression of the bond angle
D) Extent of $d\pi-p\pi$ back-bonding from hydrogen to the central atom decreases down the group
questions.explanation:
Step 1: In Group 15 hydrides ($\text{EH}_3$), the central atom possesses one lone pair and three bond pairs.
Step 2: Nitrogen has the highest electronegativity in the group; therefore, the bonding electron pairs in $\text{NH}_3$ are concentrated closer to nitrogen. The resulting high electron density causes strong bond pair-bond pair repulsion, holding the bond angle at $107.8^\circ$ (close to tetrahedral $109.5^\circ$).
Step 3: Down the group from $\text{P}$ to $\text{Sb}$, atomic size increases and electronegativity markedly decreases. Bond pair electrons are pulled less towards the central atom and lie farther away, significantly diminishing bond pair-bond pair repulsion. According to Drago's rule, bonding in $\text{PH}_3$, $\text{AsH}_3$, and $\text{SbH}_3$ involves almost pure $p$-orbitals at approximately $90^\circ$ to $94^\circ$, with the lone pair residing in an unhybridized $s$-orbital.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Hydrogen cannot participate in $d\pi-p\pi$ back-bonding as it has no available electrons/p-orbitals; steric crowding would increase bond angle rather than decrease it; and lone pair-bond pair repulsion does not induce $sp$ hybridization.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Very pure dinitrogen gas ($\text{N}_2$) containing minimal trace impurities is prepared in the laboratory by which of the following chemical reactions?
options: A) Thermal decomposition of ammonium dichromate, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$
B) Reaction of an aqueous solution of ammonium chloride with sodium nitrite ($\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NaNO}_2$)
C) Thermal decomposition of sodium azide ($\text{NaN}_3$) or barium azide ($\text{Ba(N}_3)_2$)
D) Catalytic oxidation of ammonia with atmospheric oxygen over platinum-rhodium gauze at $500\text{ K}$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Thermal decomposition of aqueous $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ with $\text{NaNO}_2$ yields $\text{N}_2$ along with small amounts of impurities such as $\text{NO}$ and $\text{HNO}_3$.
Step 2: Thermal decomposition of $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ produces $\text{N}_2$, $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$, and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Step 3: Ultra-pure dinitrogen is exclusively obtained by the gentle thermal decomposition of pure alkali or alkaline earth metal azides, specifically sodium azide ($\text{NaN}_3$) or barium azide ($\text{Ba(N}_3)_2$):
$\text{Ba(N}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Ba} + 3\text{N}_2$
$2\text{NaN}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{Na} + 3\text{N}_2$
The only by-product is the non-volatile metallic residue, yielding high-purity $\text{N}_2$ gas.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Catalytic oxidation of ammonia produces nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$), not dinitrogen (Ostwald process first step); while ammonium nitrite and ammonium dichromate yield dinitrogen contaminated with trace nitrogen oxides and solid residues.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Dinitrogen combines reversibly with dihydrogen to form ammonia according to the thermochemical equation:
$\text{N}_2(\text{g}) + 3\text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(\text{g}), \quad \Delta_r H^\circ = -92.4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
According to Le Chatelier's principle and industrial practice (Haber's process), which set of conditions maximizes the yield and rate of $\text{NH}_3$ synthesis?
options: A) Low pressure ($\approx 1\text{ atm}$), high temperature ($\approx 1200\text{ K}$), and nickel catalyst with molybdenum promoter
B) High pressure ($\approx 500\text{ atm}$), room temperature ($\approx 298\text{ K}$), and unsupported vanadium pentoxide catalyst
C) Extremely low temperature ($\approx 273\text{ K}$), low pressure ($\approx 10\text{ atm}$), and finely divided copper catalyst

D) High pressure ($\approx 200 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$ or $200\text{ atm}$), optimum temperature ($\approx 700\text{ K}$), and iron oxide catalyst with promoters $\text{K}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: The synthesis of ammonia is an exothermic reaction ($\Delta_r H^\circ = -92.4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) that proceeds with a decrease in the number of gaseous moles ($4\text{ moles} \rightarrow 2\text{ moles}$).
Step 2: According to Le Chatelier's principle, high pressure favors the forward reaction because it shifts equilibrium toward fewer moles of gas. Although low temperature favors exothermic equilibrium, the reaction rate becomes prohibitively sluggish at very low temperatures.
Step 3: Therefore, an optimum temperature of about $700\text{ K}$ is maintained along with high pressure ($\approx 200\text{ atm}$ or $200 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$). Iron oxide catalyst with small amounts of $\text{K}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is used to achieve an acceptable reaction velocity.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Low pressure disfavors product formation; room temperature kinetics are negligible without active catalysts; and $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ is the catalyst for the Contact process of sulfuric acid, not the Haber process.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Nitrogen forms several binary oxides with oxygen across various oxidation states ranging from $+1$ to $+5$. Which of the following pairs contains only neutral oxides of nitrogen?
options: A) $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{NO}$
B) $\text{NO}$ and $\text{NO}_2$
C) $\text{N}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$
D) $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{N}_2\text{O}_3$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Recall the acidity and physical states of nitrogen oxides documented in NCERT Class 12:
- Dinitrogen oxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}$, oxidation state $+1$): Colourless, neutral gas.
- Nitrogen monoxide ($\text{NO}$, oxidation state $+2$): Colourless, neutral gas.
- Dinitrogen trioxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_3$, oxidation state $+3$): Blue solid, acidic.
- Nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$, oxidation state $+4$): Brown gas, acidic.
- Dinitrogen tetroxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$, oxidation state $+4$): Colourless solid/liquid, acidic.
- Dinitrogen pentoxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$, oxidation state $+5$): Colourless solid, strongly acidic.
Step 2: Among all the oxides of nitrogen, only $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{NO}$ are neutral toward litmus paper and do not form salts with bases.
Step 3: All other oxides ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{NO}_2$, $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$, $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$) exhibit acidic properties.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Any pair containing $\text{NO}_2$, $\text{N}_2\text{O}_3$, or $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$ includes acidic oxides.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: When copper metal is treated separately with dilute and concentrated nitric acid, different gaseous reduction products of nitrogen are evolved. What are the nitrogen oxides formed in the reactions of copper with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ and concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$, respectively?
options: A) Nitrous oxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}$) with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$, and nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$) with concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$
B) Nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$) with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$, and nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$) with concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$
C) Nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$) with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$, and nitrous oxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}$) with concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$
D) Dinitrogen pentoxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$) with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$, and nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$) with concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Write the balanced redox reactions of copper metal with dilute and concentrated nitric acid as stated in NCERT:
$3\text{Cu} + 8\text{HNO}_3\text{ (dilute)} \rightarrow 3\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2 + 2\text{NO} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$
$\text{Cu} + 4\text{HNO}_3\text{ (concentrated)} \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3)_2 + 2\text{NO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$
Step 2: Notice that dilute nitric acid oxidizes copper to $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ while nitrate is reduced to nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$, oxidation state $+2$).
Step 3: Concentrated nitric acid, acting as a much stronger oxidizing agent, oxidizes copper while being reduced primarily to brown nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$, oxidation state $+4$).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ is formed when dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ reacts with zinc ($4\text{Zn} + 10\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow 4\text{Zn(NO}_3)_2 + \text{N}_2\text{O} + 5\text{H}_2\text{O}$), not copper; $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$ is never formed as a gaseous reduction product during metal dissolution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The boiling points of hydrides of Group 16 elements follow an unexpected non-monotonic sequence: $\text{H}_2\text{O} (373\text{ K}) > \text{H}_2\text{Te} (269\text{ K}) > \text{H}_2\text{Se} (232\text{ K}) > \text{H}_2\text{S} (213\text{ K})$. Which factor explains why $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ exhibits an abnormally high boiling point compared to the other members?
options: A) Higher covalent bond dissociation energy of the intramolecular $\text{O}-\text{H}$ bonds
B) Presence of empty $d$-orbitals in oxygen facilitating extensive dipole-dipole associations
C) Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding resulting from the small atomic size and high electronegativity of oxygen
D) Higher molecular weight and larger van der Waals dispersion forces in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: In Group 16 hydrides ($\text{H}_2\text{E}$), van der Waals dispersion forces increase with molecular mass from $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ to $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$, which accounts for the regular increase in boiling points from $\text{H}_2\text{S} (213\text{ K})$ to $\text{H}_2\text{Se} (232\text{ K})$ to $\text{H}_2\text{Te} (269\text{ K})$.
Step 2: However, water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) has an exceptionally high boiling point ($373\text{ K}$). This is because oxygen has a very small atomic radius and a high electronegativity ($3.5$).
Step 3: The large dipole moment and small size of oxygen enable extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding in liquid water, creating an extensive three-dimensional network that requires substantially higher thermal energy to disrupt upon vaporization.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Intramolecular covalent bond energies determine chemical stability, not boiling points; oxygen lacks $d$-orbitals entirely ($n=2$); and water has the lowest molecular weight in the group, so its van der Waals forces are the weakest.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The thermal stability of the hydrides of Group 16 elements decreases systematically from water to hydrogen telluride: $\text{H}_2\text{O} > \text{H}_2\text{S} > \text{H}_2\text{Se} > \text{H}_2\text{Te}$. What is the fundamental property governing this stability trend?
options: A) Decrease in the standard reduction potential of the central element down the group
B) Increase in the polarizability of the central element's valence shell lone pairs
C) Decrease in the $\text{H}-\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond angle from $104.5^\circ$ to $90^\circ$
D) Progressive increase in $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond length causing a decrease in $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond dissociation enthalpy
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Thermal stability of a hydride depends directly on the magnitude of the central element to hydrogen ($\text{E}-\text{H}$) bond dissociation enthalpy ($\Delta_{\text{diss}}H(\text{E}-\text{H})$).
Step 2: As the atomic size of the central chalcogen atom ($\text{E}$) increases down Group 16 ($\text{O} < \text{S} < \text{Se} < \text{Te}$), the orbital overlap between the $1s$ orbital of hydrogen and the valence $p$-orbital of $\text{E}$ becomes increasingly diffuse and less effective.
Step 3: Consequently, the $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond length increases and the bond dissociation enthalpy decreases sharply ($\text{H}_2\text{O} = 463\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $\text{H}_2\text{S} = 347\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $\text{H}_2\text{Se} = 276\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $\text{H}_2\text{Te} = 238\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$), rendering $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$ readily decomposable upon heating.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: While bond angles do decrease due to Drago's rule, the mechanical resistance to thermal cleavage is governed strictly by the bond dissociation enthalpy; polarizability affects intermolecular forces, not intramolecular bond strength.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Rhombic ($\alpha$-sulfur) and monoclinic ($\beta$-sulfur) are two crystalline allotropic forms of sulfur. At which specific transition temperature are both rhombic and monoclinic allotropes in dynamic equilibrium with each other at $1\text{ atm}$ pressure?
options: A) $369\text{ K}$
B) $393\text{ K}$
D) $312\text{ K}$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Rhombic sulfur ($\alpha$-sulfur) is the yellow crystalline allotrope that is thermodynamically stable at room temperature and transforms to monoclinic sulfur ($\beta$-sulfur) upon heating above $369\text{ K}$.
Step 2: Below $369\text{ K}$, $\alpha$-sulfur is stable, whereas above $369\text{ K}$, $\beta$-sulfur is stable.
Step 3: At exactly $369\text{ K}$, both crystalline allotropes coexist in dynamic equilibrium. This specific temperature is termed the transition temperature.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: $393\text{ K}$ is the melting point of $\beta$-sulfur ($393\text{ K}$ or $119^\circ\text{C}$); $444.6\text{ K}$ is not the transition temperature (sulfur boiling point is $717.8\text{ K}$); and $312\text{ K}$ is well within the stability range of rhombic sulfur alone.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the vapor state at elevated temperatures ($\approx 1000\text{ K}$), sulfur partly exists as diatomic $\text{S}_2$ molecules. According to molecular orbital theory, which of the following statements correctly accounts for the magnetic behavior of gaseous $\text{S}_2$?
options: A) It is diamagnetic because all valence electrons are completely paired in bonding molecular orbitals
B) It is paramagnetic because it has two unpaired electrons in degenerate $\pi^*$ antibonding molecular orbitals, analogous to $\text{O}_2$
C) It is paramagnetic due to the thermal excitation of a single electron from an $s$-orbital to a vacant $d$-orbital
D) It is diamagnetic because sulfur vaporizes exclusively as puckered cyclic $\text{S}_8$ rings at $1000\text{ K}$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: At high temperatures around $1000\text{ K}$, the puckered $\text{S}_8$ rings dissociate into smaller fragments, with $\text{S}_2$ being the dominant gaseous species.
Step 2: The diatomic $\text{S}_2$ molecule has $16$ valence electrons (like $\text{O}_2$) and is isoelectronic with dioxygen in its valence shell configuration:
$\sigma_{3s}^2 \sigma^*_{3s}^2 \sigma_{3p_z}^2 (\pi_{3p_x}^2 = \pi_{3p_y}^2) (\pi^*_{3p_x}^1 = \pi^*_{3p_y}^1)$.
Step 3: In accordance with Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity, the two highest energy valence electrons occupy the degenerate antibonding $\pi^*_{3p_x}$ and $\pi^*_{3p_y}$ orbitals with parallel spins, imparting paramagnetism to $\text{S}_2$.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: $\text{S}_2$ is paramagnetic, not diamagnetic; the paramagnetism originates from molecular orbital occupancy rather than promotional $s \rightarrow d$ atomic excitation; and $\text{S}_8$ rings break down significantly above the boiling point ($718\text{ K}$).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the industrial manufacture of sulfuric acid via the Contact process, sulfur trioxide ($\text{SO}_3$) gas produced by catalytic oxidation of $\text{SO}_2$ over $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ is absorbed in concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ rather than directly into water. What is the fundamental technological reason for this procedure?
options: A) The direct dissolution of $\text{SO}_3$ in water is an endothermic process with an unfavorable Gibbs free energy change
B) $\text{SO}_3$ does not react with water unless an alkali metal sulfate catalyst is present in the medium
C) Direct absorption of $\text{SO}_3$ in water is highly exothermic and generates a dense, unmanageable acid mist/fog that resists condensation
D) Reaction of $\text{SO}_3$ with water causes thermal decomposition of sulfuric acid back into $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: The key step in the Contact process produces sulfur trioxide:
$2\text{SO}_2(\text{g}) + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) \xrightarrow{\text{V}_2\text{O}_5} 2\text{SO}_3(\text{g})$
Step 2: When $\text{SO}_3$ reacts with liquid water, the reaction is violently exothermic. The enormous heat liberated instantaneously vaporizes water, forming tiny droplets of sulfuric acid suspended in gas—a dense, persistent acid mist/fog.
Step 3: This colloidal acid fog does not condense easily and passes out with exhaust gases, creating severe pollution and low recovery yields. Hence, $\text{SO}_3$ is absorbed smoothly into $98\%$ concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to yield oleum ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7$), which is subsequently diluted with calculated amounts of water to yield sulfuric acid of the desired concentration.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: The reaction of $\text{SO}_3$ with water has a strongly negative Gibbs energy (highly spontaneous and exothermic, not endothermic); no alkali metal sulfate catalyst is needed; and sulfuric acid does not dissociate back into $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ under these ambient absorption conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The negative electron gain enthalpy ($\Delta_{eg}H$) of chlorine ($-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) is unexpectedly more negative than that of fluorine ($-333\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$), despite fluorine having a higher electronegativity. Which of the following factors is the direct cause of this anomaly?
options: A) Fluorine has empty $d$-orbitals that accept electron density and cause extensive orbital contraction
B) Chlorine has a lower nuclear charge, which allows easier approach of an additional electron
C) The $\text{F}-\text{F}$ bond dissociation enthalpy is significantly higher than that of the $\text{Cl}-\text{Cl}$ bond
D) The extremely compact $2p$ subshell of fluorine experiences strong interelectronic repulsions, which destabilize the incoming electron
questions.explanation:
Step 1: When an electron is added to an isolated halogen atom in the gaseous state, energy is released:
$\text{X}(\text{g}) + e^- \rightarrow \text{X}^-(\text{g})$.
Step 2: Although fluorine has a higher effective nuclear charge and smaller radius, its valence electrons are confined to the very compact and tiny $2p$ orbitals ($n=2$).
Step 3: As a result, the incoming electron experiences intense interelectronic repulsion from the existing six $2p$ electrons. In chlorine, the incoming electron enters the larger, more dispersed $3p$ orbital where interelectronic repulsions are significantly weaker, releasing more energy ($-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for $\text{Cl}$ vs $-333\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for $\text{F}$).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Fluorine belongs to period 2 and possesses no $d$-orbitals; chlorine has a higher nuclear charge ($Z=17$) than fluorine ($Z=9$); and the $\text{F}-\text{F}$ bond dissociation enthalpy is lower, not higher, than that of $\text{Cl}-\text{Cl}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The bond dissociation enthalpies ($\Delta_{\text{bond}}H^\circ$) of diatomic halogen molecules follow the order: $\text{Cl}_2 (242.6\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) > \text{Br}_2 (192.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) > \text{F}_2 (158.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) > \text{I}_2 (151.1\text{ kJ mol}^{-1})$. Why is the $\text{F}-\text{F}$ bond dissociation enthalpy abnormally lower than those of $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{Br}_2$?
options: A) Intense electrostatic repulsion between the non-bonding valence lone pairs on the two small, closely spaced fluorine atoms
B) Formation of weak hydrogen bonding between adjacent fluorine molecules
C) Participation of valence $d$-orbitals in chlorine and bromine that dramatically shortens their covalent bonds
D) Hyperconjugation across the halogen-halogen single covalent bond
questions.explanation:
Step 1: In diatomic halogen molecules ($\text{X}_2$), each atom holds three non-bonding lone pairs of electrons.
Step 2: Due to the extremely small atomic radius of fluorine, the two bonded fluorine atoms are brought very close to one another ($\text{F}-\text{F}$ bond distance is only $142\text{ pm}$).
Step 3: Consequently, the non-bonding electron pairs on the two adjacent fluorine atoms experience severe lone pair-lone pair electrostatic repulsions, weakening the single covalent bond. In $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{Br}_2$, the larger internuclear separation reduces lone pair repulsions, resulting in higher bond dissociation enthalpies ($\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{F}_2 > \text{I}_2$).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Diatomic halogen molecules cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds; halogens do not exhibit hyperconjugation; and $d$-orbitals in chlorine do not shorten single covalent bonds.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Which of the following correctly lists the hydrogen halides ($\text{HX}$) in order of increasing acidic strength in aqueous solution, along with the correct underlying reason?
options: A) $\text{HI} < \text{HBr} < \text{HCl} < \text{HF}$, because fluorine has the highest electronegativity to pull protons away
B) $\text{HF} < \text{HCl} < \text{HBr} < \text{HI}$, because the $\text{H}-\text{X}$ bond dissociation enthalpy decreases from $\text{HF}$ to $\text{HI}$
C) $\text{HF} < \text{HCl} < \text{HBr} < \text{HI}$, because the hydration enthalpy of halide ions increases down the group
D) $\text{HCl} < \text{HF} < \text{HBr} < \text{HI}$, because $\text{HF}$ is a weak acid due to high polarizability of fluoride
questions.explanation:
Step 1: The acidic strength of hydrogen halides ($\text{HX}$) in aqueous solution depends on their ability to dissociate into $\text{H}^+(\text{aq})$ and $\text{X}^-(\text{aq})$.
Step 2: The dominant thermodynamic factor dictating proton release down Group 17 is the bond dissociation enthalpy of the $\text{H}-\text{X}$ bond:
$\Delta_{\text{diss}}H^\circ(\text{H}-\text{F}) = 574\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$,
$\Delta_{\text{diss}}H^\circ(\text{H}-\text{Cl}) = 432\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$,
$\Delta_{\text{diss}}H^\circ(\text{H}-\text{Br}) = 363\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$,
$\Delta_{\text{diss}}H^\circ(\text{H}-\text{I}) = 295\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
Step 3: As atomic size increases from $\text{F}$ to $\text{I}$, the $\text{H}-\text{X}$ bond length increases and the bond dissociation energy decreases markedly. Thus, the cleavage of the $\text{H}-\text{I}$ bond occurs most readily, making $\text{HI}$ the strongest acid and $\text{HF}$ the weakest acid ($\text{HF} < \text{HCl} < \text{HBr} < \text{HI}$).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Electronegativity would predict $\text{HF}$ to be strongest, but experimental bond cleavage energy overrides polarity; and hydration enthalpy actually decreases from $\text{F}^-$ to $\text{I}^-$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Chlorine trifluoride ($\text{ClF}_3$) is an interhalogen compound widely used in the production of uranium hexafluoride. According to VSEPR theory, what are the hybridization of the central chlorine atom and the molecular geometry of $\text{ClF}_3$?
options: A) $sp^3$ hybridization and trigonal pyramidal geometry with one lone pair
B) $sp^3d^2$ hybridization and trigonal bipyramidal geometry with no lone pairs
C) $sp^3d$ hybridization and T-shaped geometry with two equatorial lone pairs
D) $dsp^2$ hybridization and square planar geometry with two axial lone pairs
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Determine the total number of valence shell electron pairs around the central chlorine atom in $\text{ClF}_3$:
Chlorine has 7 valence electrons, shares 3 electrons with three fluorine atoms, leaving 4 non-bonding electrons (2 lone pairs).
$\text{Steric Number} = 3\text{ bond pairs} + 2\text{ lone pairs} = 5$.
Step 2: A steric number of 5 corresponds to $sp^3d$ hybridization with a trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry.
Step 3: According to VSEPR theory, lone pairs occupy the equatorial positions to minimize $90^\circ$ lone pair-bond pair repulsions. With two equatorial lone pairs and three bond pairs (one equatorial, two axial), the observed molecular geometry is bent T-shaped.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Trigonal pyramidal requires steric number 4 ($sp^3$); square planar requires steric number 6 with two trans lone pairs ($sp^3d^2$); and $dsp^2$ is typical of $d^8$ transition metal complexes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the interhalogen compound bromine pentafluoride ($\text{BrF}_5$), what are the hybridization of the central bromine atom and its molecular geometry according to VSEPR theory?
options: A) $sp^3d$ hybridization and trigonal bipyramidal geometry
B) $sp^3d^3$ hybridization and pentagonal planar geometry
C) $sp^3d^2$ hybridization and octahedral geometry
D) $sp^3d^2$ hybridization and square pyramidal geometry
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Bromine has 7 valence electrons. In $\text{BrF}_5$, it forms 5 single covalent bonds with fluorine atoms, leaving $7 - 5 = 2$ non-bonding valence electrons (1 lone pair).
Step 2: $\text{Steric Number} = 5\text{ bond pairs} + 1\text{ lone pair} = 6$.
Step 3: A steric number of 6 corresponds to $sp^3d^2$ hybridization with an octahedral electron pair arrangement. With 5 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair occupying one axial vertex, the molecular geometry is square pyramidal.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Octahedral describes the electron-pair geometry rather than the molecular geometry; trigonal bipyramidal corresponds to steric number 5 ($sp^3d$); and pentagonal planar corresponds to steric number 7 ($sp^3d^3$) with two lone pairs.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In 1962, Neil Bartlett synthesized the first true chemical compound of a noble gas, $[\text{Xe}]^+[\text{PtF}_6]^-$. What critical piece of experimental data prompted Bartlett to attempt the reaction between xenon and platinum hexafluoride ($\text{PtF}_6$)?
options: A) The first ionization enthalpy of molecular oxygen ($\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{O}_2^+$, $1175\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) is remarkably close to that of xenon ($1170\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$)
B) Xenon has an identical atomic radius to that of platinum
C) The electron gain enthalpy of xenon is equal in magnitude to that of fluorine
D) Molecular oxygen and xenon have identical electronegativities on the Pauling scale
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Neil Bartlett first prepared the ionic compound $\text{O}_2^+[\text{PtF}_6]^-$ by reacting dioxygen with the powerful oxidizing agent platinum hexafluoride ($\text{PtF}_6$).
Step 2: He realized that the first ionization enthalpy of molecular oxygen ($\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{O}_2^+ + e^-$) is $1175\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
Step 3: Looking up atomic data, Bartlett noticed that xenon has a first ionization enthalpy of $1170\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, almost identical to that of $\text{O}_2$. He reasoned that $\text{PtF}_6$ should therefore also be capable of oxidizing xenon, and upon mixing xenon and $\text{PtF}_6$, an orange-yellow solid $[\text{Xe}]^+[\text{PtF}_6]^-$ was successfully obtained.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Atomic radius matching was not the thermodynamic driver; noble gases have positive electron gain enthalpies; and oxygen and xenon have very different electronegativity values.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Xenon difluoride ($\text{XeF}_2$) is synthesized directly by the thermal reaction between xenon and fluorine gases under which of the following specific stoichiometric and experimental conditions?
options: A) Fluorine in excess ($\text{Xe} : \text{F}_2$ molar ratio of $1 : 5$) at $873\text{ K}$ and $7\text{ bar}$ pressure
B) Xenon in excess ($\text{Xe} : \text{F}_2$ molar ratio of $2 : 1$) at $673\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ bar}$ pressure
C) High excess of fluorine ($\text{Xe} : \text{F}_2$ molar ratio of $1 : 20$) at $573\text{ K}$ and $60-70\text{ bar}$ pressure
D) Equimolar mixture of $\text{Xe}$ and $\text{F}_2$ at $298\text{ K}$ and $100\text{ bar}$ pressure with an iron catalyst
questions.explanation:
Step 1: The three xenon binary fluorides are prepared under distinct conditions of molar ratios, temperatures, and pressures as cataloged in NCERT Chemistry Class 12:
- $\text{XeF}_2$: $\text{Xe}(\text{g}) + \text{F}_2(\text{g}) \xrightarrow{673\text{ K}, 1\text{ bar}} \text{XeF}_2(\text{s})$ with xenon in excess ($\text{Xe} : \text{F}_2 = 2 : 1$).
- $\text{XeF}_4$: $\text{Xe}(\text{g}) + 2\text{F}_2(\text{g}) \xrightarrow{873\text{ K}, 7\text{ bar}} \text{XeF}_4(\text{s})$ with $\text{Xe} : \text{F}_2 = 1 : 5$.
- $\text{XeF}_6$: $\text{Xe}(\text{g}) + 3\text{F}_2(\text{g}) \xrightarrow{573\text{ K}, 60-70\text{ bar}} \text{XeF}_6(\text{s})$ with $\text{Xe} : \text{F}_2 = 1 : 20$.
Step 2: Therefore, synthesizing $\text{XeF}_2$ specifically requires an excess of xenon ($\text{Xe} : \text{F}_2 = 2 : 1$) at $673\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ bar}$.
Step 3: Excess fluorine and higher pressures drive the reaction toward the higher fluorides $\text{XeF}_4$ and $\text{XeF}_6$.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: A $1:5$ ratio at $873\text{ K}$ yields $\text{XeF}_4$; a $1:20$ ratio at $60-70\text{ bar}$ yields $\text{XeF}_6$; and no reaction occurs between $\text{Xe}$ and $\text{F}_2$ at room temperature ($298\text{ K}$).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: What are the state of hybridization of the central xenon atom and the molecular shape of xenon tetrafluoride ($\text{XeF}_4$), according to VSEPR theory?
options: A) $sp^3d$ hybridization and see-saw shape with one equatorial lone pair
B) $sp^3$ hybridization and tetrahedral shape with no lone pairs
C) $sp^3d^2$ hybridization and square planar shape with two lone pairs occupying mutually trans axial positions
D) $sp^3d^2$ hybridization and tetrahedral shape with two cis lone pairs
questions.explanation:
Step 1: In $\text{XeF}_4$, xenon possesses 8 valence electrons. It forms 4 single covalent $\sigma$-bonds with four fluorine atoms, leaving $8 - 4 = 4$ non-bonding valence electrons, which constitute 2 lone pairs.
Step 2: $\text{Steric Number} = 4\text{ bond pairs} + 2\text{ lone pairs} = 6$.
Step 3: A steric number of 6 corresponds to $sp^3d^2$ hybridization with an octahedral arrangement of electron pairs. To minimize electrostatic lone pair-lone pair repulsions ($180^\circ$ separation), the two lone pairs reside at mutually opposite (trans) axial positions, while the four fluorine atoms lie in the equatorial plane, yielding a square planar molecular geometry.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: See-saw geometry corresponds to steric number 5 with one lone pair ($sp^3d$); tetrahedral corresponds to steric number 4 ($sp^3$); and placing lone pairs in cis positions in an octahedral frame causes severe $90^\circ$ repulsions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Xenon trioxide ($\text{XeO}_3$) is a colourless, explosive solid formed by the complete hydrolysis of xenon hexafluoride. What is the hybridization and molecular shape of $\text{XeO}_3$?
options: A) $sp^2$ hybridization and trigonal planar shape
B) $sp^3d$ hybridization and T-shaped geometry
C) $sp^3d^2$ hybridization and square planar shape
D) $sp^3$ hybridization and trigonal pyramidal shape
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Xenon has 8 valence electrons. In $\text{XeO}_3$, each oxygen atom forms a double bond ($\sigma + \pi$) with xenon.
Step 2: Xenon forms three $\sigma$-bonds with the three oxygen atoms and retains one non-bonding lone pair ($8 - 3 \times 2 = 2$ electrons).
Step 3: $\text{Steric Number} = 3\text{ }\sigma\text{-bonds} + 1\text{ lone pair} = 4$.
Steric number 4 corresponds to $sp^3$ hybridization. With three bonding directions and one lone pair, the molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal, isostructural with the iodate ion ($\text{IO}_3^-$). The multiple bonding involves xenon's empty $5d$ orbitals and oxygen's filled $2p$ orbitals ($d\pi-p\pi$ bonding).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Trigonal planar requires 3 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs ($sp^2$); T-shaped requires steric number 5 ($sp^3d$); and square planar requires steric number 6 ($sp^3d^2$).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: When concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid cane sugar (sucrose, $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}$), the mass turns black and swells into a porous, spongy carbonaceous cylinder with the evolution of steam. This dramatic reaction demonstrates which chemical property of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$?
options: A) Strong dehydrating agent, removing water elements ($\text{H}$ and $\text{O}$) in a $2:1$ atomic ratio from organic compounds
B) Powerful reducing agent, reducing carbon to its elemental black state
C) Strong halogenating agent, displacing hydroxyl groups from the sucrose ring
D) Hydrolytic catalyst, converting polysaccharide rings into gaseous carbon monoxide
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Concentrated sulfuric acid has an exceptionally strong affinity for water ($\Delta_{\text{mix}}H^\circ$ is very large and negative).
Step 2: When concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ comes into contact with carbohydrates such as sucrose, glucose, or cellulose, it extracts hydrogen and oxygen in the atomic ratio of $2:1$ (as water) from the molecular structure:
$\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}\text{ (s)} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} 12\text{C}\text{ (s)} + 11\text{H}_2\text{O}\text{ (g)}$
Step 3: The intense heat liberated converts the extracted water into steam, which puffs up the resulting elemental black carbon into a spongy mass. This process is called the charring of sugar and illustrates the powerful dehydrating property of concentrated sulfuric acid.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acts as an oxidizing agent, not a reducing agent; no halogens are present in the system; and sucrose is dehydrated to elemental carbon rather than hydrolyzed to carbon monoxide.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Nitrogen has an electronic configuration of $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$. While heavier Group 15 elements like phosphorus form pentahalides such as $\text{PCl}_5$, nitrogen never forms $\text{NCl}_5$ or $\text{NF}_5$, and its maximum covalency is strictly restricted to 4. What is the fundamental atomic factor responsible for this restriction?
options: A) Unusually high electronegativity of nitrogen preventing bond formation with halogens
B) Absence of vacant $d$-orbitals in the valence shell ($n=2$) of nitrogen
C) Inability of nitrogen to form $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds with halogens
D) High positive electron gain enthalpy of nitrogen
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Nitrogen is in the second period ($n=2$) of the periodic table, where the valence shell consists exclusively of one $2s$ orbital and three $2p$ orbitals.
Step 2: Because the principal quantum number $n=2$ has no $d$ subshell ($l$ can only be $0$ or $1$), there are altogether only four valence orbitals available for bonding.
Step 3: Consequently, nitrogen can expand its octet to accommodate a maximum of four electron pairs (covalency of 4, as seen in $\text{NH}_4^+$), and cannot expand its coordination number to form pentahalides like $\text{NCl}_5$ or $\text{NF}_5$. Heavier elements like phosphorus ($n=3$) possess accessible vacant $3d$ orbitals, permitting expansion of their octet to form hexacoordinate and pentacoordinate species.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Electronegativity does not restrict orbital availability for covalent bonding; nitrogen's ability to form $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds is characteristic of its chemistry but does not limit its maximum covalency; and electron gain enthalpy describes anion formation rather than maximum covalency.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding the chemical properties of Group 15 hydrides:
Statement I: Ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) is the strongest Lewis base among Group 15 hydrides, and basic strength progressively decreases down the group to bismuthine ($\text{BiH}_3$).
Statement II: Bismuthine ($\text{BiH}_3$) is the strongest reducing agent among Group 15 hydrides because the $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond dissociation enthalpy is lowest for bismuth.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
C) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Statement I: Group 15 hydrides act as Lewis bases due to the presence of a lone pair of electrons on the central atom. As atomic size increases down the group from $\text{N}$ to $\text{Bi}$, the lone pair occupies a progressively larger, more diffuse orbital. Hence, the electron density on nitrogen is highest, making $\text{NH}_3$ the most facile electron-pair donor (strongest Lewis base). Thus, Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Analyze Statement II: Reducing strength is governed by the ease of $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond cleavage. Down the group, the $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond length increases and the bond dissociation enthalpy decreases sharply ($\text{Bi}-\text{H}$ bond is the longest and weakest). Consequently, $\text{BiH}_3$ liberates hydrogen atoms most readily, acting as the strongest reducing agent among Group 15 hydrides. Thus, Statement II is correct.
Step 3: Since both statements are factually sound and fully substantiated by periodic trends, both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Any assertion claiming that either statement is incorrect overlooks the fundamental roles of lone pair density in basicity and bond enthalpy in reducing power.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Bismuth pentafluoride ($\text{BiF}_5$) is a well-characterized, stable compound, whereas bismuth pentachloride ($\text{BiCl}_5$) does not exist.
Reason (R): Due to the inert pair effect, the $+5$ oxidation state of bismuth is strongly oxidizing, and only the small, highly electronegative fluorine atom with high oxidizing power can stabilize $\text{Bi(V)}$ without being oxidized by it.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: A) (A) is false but (R) is true
B) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
C) (A) is true but (R) is false
D) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Assertion (A): In Group 15, bismuth displays a stable $+3$ oxidation state. However, with fluorine, bismuth forms $\text{BiF}_5$, whereas other pentahalides like $\text{BiCl}_5$, $\text{BiBr}_5$, and $\text{BiI}_5$ are unknown. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.
Step 2: Analyze Reason (R): Due to the inert pair effect (poor shielding of $6s^2$ electrons by intervening $4f^{14}$ and $5d^{10}$ shells), $\text{Bi(V)}$ is energetically unstable and acts as a powerful oxidizing agent. Chloride, bromide, and iodide ions are readily oxidized by $\text{Bi(V)}$ to elemental halogens, reducing $\text{Bi(V)}$ to stable $\text{Bi(III)}$. Only fluorine, being the most electronegative element with an extremely high oxidation potential ($E^\circ = +2.87\text{ V}$), cannot be oxidized by $\text{Bi(V)}$, thereby stabilizing the $+5$ oxidation state in $\text{BiF}_5$. Thus, Reason (R) is true.
Step 3: Reason (R) directly explains the existence of $\text{BiF}_5$ and the non-existence of $\text{BiCl}_5$. Hence, both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Alternatives stating that (A) or (R) is false or that (R) is not explanatory fail to recognize the thermodynamic balance between the oxidizing capacity of $\text{Bi(V)}$ and the reducing capacity of halide ions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the brown ring test for nitrate ions ($\text{NO}_3^-$), the appearance of a brown ring at the liquid-liquid junction is caused by the formation of a coordination entity. What is the chemical formula of this brown ring complex, and what are the oxidation state of iron and the formal charge on the nitric oxide ligand within it?
options: A) $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5(\text{NO})]^{2+}$, where iron is in $+1$ oxidation state and nitric oxide is coordinated as $\text{NO}^+$
B) $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5(\text{NO})]^{3+}$, where iron is in $+3$ oxidation state and nitric oxide is coordinated as neutral $\text{NO}$
C) $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4(\text{NO})_2]^{2+}$, where iron is in $+2$ oxidation state and nitric oxide is coordinated as $\text{NO}^-$
D) $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5(\text{NO}_2)]^{2+}$, where iron is in $+2$ oxidation state and ligand is nitrosonium $\text{NO}_2^+$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: The brown ring test involves reduction of nitrate ion ($\text{NO}_3^-$) by ferrous sulfate in an acidic medium:
$\text{NO}_3^- + 3\text{Fe}^{2+} + 4\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{NO} + 3\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Step 2: The generated nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$) displaces one aqua ligand from the hydrated ferrous ion:
$[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + \text{NO} \rightarrow [\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5(\text{NO})]^{2+} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Step 3: In this pentaaquanitrosyliron(I) cation, an electron is transferred from the $\pi^*$ orbital of neutral $\text{NO}$ to the iron center, formally reducing iron from $\text{Fe(II)}$ to $\text{Fe(I)}$ ($d^7$, with 3 unpaired electrons and a magnetic moment of $\approx 3.87\text{ BM}$) while the nitric oxide ligand acquires a $+1$ charge as nitrosonium ($\text{NO}^+$).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Complexes featuring $\text{Fe(III)}$ or two nitrosyl ligands are incorrect; and $\text{NO}_2^+$ is the nitronium ion found in nitrating mixtures, not the nitrosyl ligand of the brown ring.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding the reactions of zinc metal with nitric acid ($\text{HNO}_3$):
Statement I: When zinc reacts with dilute (approx. $20\%$) nitric acid, the primary gaseous nitrogen-containing reduction product is nitrous oxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}$).
Statement II: When zinc reacts with concentrated (approx. $70\%$) nitric acid, the primary gaseous reduction product is nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$).
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Examine Statement I: The stoichiometric reaction of zinc with dilute nitric acid is:
$4\text{Zn} + 10\text{HNO}_3\text{ (dilute)} \rightarrow 4\text{Zn(NO}_3)_2 + 5\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{N}_2\text{O}$.
The nitrate ion is reduced from $+5$ down to $+1$ in nitrous oxide (laughing gas, $\text{N}_2\text{O}$). Thus, Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Examine Statement II: The reaction of zinc with concentrated nitric acid proceeds as:
$\text{Zn} + 4\text{HNO}_3\text{ (concentrated)} \rightarrow \text{Zn(NO}_3)_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{NO}_2$.
In concentrated acid, nitrate is reduced to brown nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$, oxidation state $+4$). Thus, Statement II is correct.
Step 3: Both statements correctly reflect the established NCERT Class 12 chemical equations for the reduction products of nitric acid on zinc.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Confusing zinc's dilute reaction product ($\text{N}_2\text{O}$) with copper's dilute product ($\text{NO}$) is a frequent student error; both statements here are fully accurate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding the oxides of nitrogen:
I. Nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$) is an odd-electron molecule and paramagnetic in the gaseous phase, but diamagnetic in liquid and solid phases due to loose dimerization into $\text{N}_2\text{O}_2$.
II. Nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$) is a brown, paramagnetic gas containing an odd electron that dimerizes readily to colourless, diamagnetic $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$.
III. Solid dinitrogen pentoxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$) does not exist as covalent molecules, but crystallizes as an ionic compound composed of nitronium cation $[\text{NO}_2]^+$ and nitrate anion $[\text{NO}_3]^-$.
IV. Dinitrogen trioxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_3$) is an acidic blue solid obtained by condensing equimolar proportions of $\text{NO}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ at $250\text{ K}$.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: A) I, II, and III only
B) II and IV only
C) I, II, III, and IV
D) I and III only
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Statement I: $\text{NO}$ contains 11 valence electrons. The unshared odd electron in its $\pi^*_{2p}$ orbital causes paramagnetism in gas; upon cooling, it pairs up to form loose planar dimers ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_2$), rendering liquid and solid states diamagnetic. (Statement I is correct).
Step 2: Statement II: $\text{NO}_2$ has 17 valence electrons with an odd electron on nitrogen. To achieve pairing, it dimerizes to $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$, which has a planar structure with a central $\text{N}-\text{N}$ bond and is diamagnetic. (Statement II is correct).
Step 3: Statement III: In the crystalline solid state, $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$ undergoes self-ionization to form the ionic lattice $[\text{NO}_2]^+[\text{NO}_3]^-$ (nitronium nitrate), where $[\text{NO}_2]^+$ is linear and $[\text{NO}_3]^-$ is trigonal planar. (Statement III is correct).
Step 4: Statement IV: Equimolar combination of $\text{NO}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ at $-23^\circ\text{C}$ ($250\text{ K}$) yields dinitrogen trioxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_3$), which is an intense blue acidic liquid/solid. (Statement IV is correct). Consequently, all four statements (I, II, III, and IV) are correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Match List I (Oxoacid of Sulfur) with List II (Characteristic Structural Feature / Linkage):
List I:
A. Peroxodisulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_8$)
B. Pyrosulfuric acid / Oleum ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7$)
C. Thiosulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3$)
D. Peroxomonosulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_5$)

List II:
1. Contains one $-\text{S}-\text{O}-\text{O}-\text{H}$ peroxy group and sulfur in $+6$ oxidation state
2. Contains one bridging $-\text{S}-\text{O}-\text{S}-$ bond with both sulfur atoms in $+6$ oxidation state
3. Contains one bridging $-\text{O}-\text{O}-$ peroxy linkage connecting two sulfur atoms in $+6$ oxidation states
4. Contains a terminal $\text{S}=\text{S}$ double bond replacing one oxo oxygen atom in sulfuric acid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Match A: Peroxodisulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_8$, Marshall's acid) consists of two tetrahedral $\text{SO}_3\text{H}$ units joined by a peroxy bridge ($-\text{O}-\text{O}-$). Both sulfur atoms have an oxidation state of $+6$. Hence, A matches with 3.
Step 2: Match B: Pyrosulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7$, oleum) consists of two $\text{SO}_3\text{H}$ units linked by a bridging oxygen atom ($-\text{S}-\text{O}-\text{S}-$). Hence, B matches with 2.
Step 3: Match C: Thiosulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3$) is derived from $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ by replacing one oxygen atom with a sulfur atom, featuring a terminal $\text{S}=\text{S}$ double bond. Hence, C matches with 4.
Step 4: Match D: Peroxomonosulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_5$, Caro's acid) contains one peroxy monosulfate linkage ($-\text{S}-\text{O}-\text{O}-\text{H}$) with sulfur in $+6$. Hence, D matches with 1. Therefore, the correct matching is A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Atmospheric ozone ($\text{O}_3$) can be quantitatively estimated using excess potassium iodide solution buffered with a borate buffer.
Reason (R): Ozone liberates iodine quantitatively from neutral $\text{KI}$ solution according to the reaction $\text{O}_3 + 2\text{I}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + \text{I}_2 + 2\text{OH}^-$, and the liberated $\text{I}_2$ is titrated against standard sodium thiosulfate solution.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: A) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
B) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
C) (A) is true but (R) is false
D) (A) is false but (R) is true
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Assertion (A): Quantitative estimation of ozone is standardly conducted in analytical laboratories by absorbing ozone into an aqueous solution of potassium iodide buffered with a borate buffer at $\text{pH} = 9.2$. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.
Step 2: Analyze Reason (R): Ozone is a powerful oxidizing agent due to the ease with which it liberates nascent oxygen: $\text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + [\text{O}]$. In the presence of excess $\text{I}^-$ and water, ozone oxidizes iodide ions quantitatively to molecular iodine ($\text{I}_2$):
$\text{O}_3 + 2\text{I}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + \text{I}_2 + 2\text{OH}^-$.
The stoichiometric amount of liberated iodine is subsequently titrated against a standardized sodium thiosulfate ($\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3$) solution using starch indicator. Thus, Reason (R) is true.
Step 3: Reason (R) provides the exact chemical reaction and titration protocol that explains the quantitative analytical method described in Assertion (A). Hence, both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Statements denying the truth of (A) or (R) or the explanatory relationship contradict standard NCERT Class 12 methodology for ozone estimation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding the oxoacids of halogens:
Statement I: Among the oxoacids of chlorine, the acidic strength increases in the sequence: $\text{HClO} < \text{HClO}_2 < \text{HClO}_3 < \text{HClO}_4$.
Statement II: The increase in acidic strength from $\text{HClO}$ to $\text{HClO}_4$ occurs because the conjugate base is progressively stabilized by delocalization of negative charge over a greater number of electronegative oxygen atoms via resonance.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Statement I: The oxoacids of chlorine feature chlorine in oxidation states $+1$ ($\text{HClO}$), $+3$ ($\text{HClO}_2$), $+5$ ($\text{HClO}_3$), and $+7$ ($\text{HClO}_4$). The acid dissociation constant ($K_a$) increases dramatically from hypochlorous acid to perchloric acid, making $\text{HClO}_4$ one of the strongest inorganic acids. Thus, Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Analyze Statement II: Deprotonation yields the conjugate bases $\text{ClO}^-$, $\text{ClO}_2^-$, $\text{ClO}_3^-$, and $\text{ClO}_4^-$. In the perchlorate ion ($\text{ClO}_4^-$), the negative charge is delocalized over four equivalent oxygen atoms through resonance across four canonical forms, resulting in the lowest formal charge per oxygen atom ($-0.25$) and maximum electrostatic stability. In $\text{ClO}^-$, the negative charge is concentrated on a single oxygen atom. Thus, Statement II is correct.
Step 3: Since both statements are chemically accurate and Statement II provides the theoretical rationale for Statement I, both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Option variants claiming that acidic strength decreases with oxidation state fail to account for conjugate base resonance stabilization.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Fluorine forms only a single known oxoacid, hypofluorous acid ($\text{HOF}$), whereas chlorine forms a series of oxoacids ($\text{HClO}$, $\text{HClO}_2$, $\text{HClO}_3$, $\text{HClO}_4$).
Reason (R): Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of all elements and completely lacks vacant $d$-orbitals in its valence shell ($n=2$), which prevents it from expanding its coordination number or exhibiting higher positive oxidation states.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: A) (A) is true but (R) is false
B) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
C) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
D) (A) is false but (R) is true
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Assertion (A): Chlorine, bromine, and iodine form multiple series of oxoacids in oxidation states $+1$, $+3$, $+5$, and $+7$. In contrast, fluorine forms only one oxoacid, $\text{HOF}$ (hypofluorous acid, also named fluoric(I) acid). Thus, Assertion (A) is true.
Step 2: Analyze Reason (R): Formation of higher oxoacids (such as $\text{HXO}_2$, $\text{HXO}_3$, and $\text{HXO}_4$) requires the halogen to exhibit higher oxidation states and expand its valence octet by utilizing vacant $d$-orbitals. Because fluorine is a second-period element with only $2s$ and $2p$ subshells, it has no accessible $d$-orbitals. Furthermore, being the most electronegative element, oxygen cannot polarize electron density away from fluorine to generate positive formal charges. Thus, Reason (R) is true.
Step 3: Reason (R) directly explains the structural and electronic limitations of fluorine in forming only $\text{HOF}$. Hence, both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Any assertion that $\text{HOF}$ is not an oxoacid or that fluorine possesses $d$-orbitals contradicts basic quantum mechanical principles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Which of the following statements regarding interhalogen compounds ($\text{XX}'_n$, where $\text{X}$ is the larger halogen and $\text{X}'$ is the smaller halogen) are correct?
I. Interhalogen compounds are generally more reactive than pure halogens, with the sole exception of fluorine ($\text{F}_2$).
II. The higher reactivity of interhalogens relative to pure halogens arises because the heteroatomic $\text{X}-\text{X}'$ bond is weaker and more polar than the homoatomic $\text{X}-\text{X}$ bond (except $\text{F}-\text{F}$).
III. Hydrolysis of an interhalogen compound $\text{XX}'$ always produces a halide ion derived from the smaller halogen $\text{X}'$ and an oxohalate/hypohalite derived from the larger halogen $\text{X}$.
IV. All interhalogen compounds are covalent and diamagnetic in nature.
Choose the correct option:
options: A) I and III only
B) II and IV only
C) I, II, and IV only
D) I, II, III, and IV
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Statement I & II: Interhalogen compounds are more reactive than halogens except fluorine because the polar $\text{X}-\text{X}'$ covalent bond has lower bond dissociation energy than homoatomic $\text{X}-\text{X}$ bonds in $\text{Cl}_2$, $\text{Br}_2$, and $\text{I}_2$. Fluorine is an exception because of the anomalously low $\text{F}-\text{F}$ bond strength caused by lone pair-lone pair repulsions. (Statements I and II are correct).
Step 2: Statement III: Upon hydrolysis, the more electronegative smaller halogen $\text{X}'$ retains the negative oxidation state to form halide ($\text{X}'^-$ or $\text{HX}'$), while the less electronegative larger halogen $\text{X}$ maintains its positive oxidation state to form an oxoacid or oxohalate (for instance, $\text{BrF}_5 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 5\text{HF} + \text{HBrO}_3$). (Statement III is correct).
Step 3: Statement IV: In interhalogen molecules, all electrons are paired up into bonding and non-bonding electron pairs; hence, they are covalent and diamagnetic. (Statement IV is correct).
Step 4: Consequently, all four statements (I, II, III, and IV) are correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Complete hydrolysis of xenon tetrafluoride ($\text{XeF}_4$) with water does not yield a single binary oxide, but instead undergoes a redox disproportionation reaction. What are the stoichiometric reaction products formed upon complete hydrolysis of $\text{XeF}_4$?
options: A) Elemental xenon ($\text{Xe}$), xenon trioxide ($\text{XeO}_3$), hydrofluoric acid ($\text{HF}$), and dioxygen ($\text{O}_2$)
B) Xenon dioxide ($\text{XeO}_2$) and hydrofluoric acid ($\text{HF}$) only
C) Xenon trioxide ($\text{XeO}_3$) and hydrofluoric acid ($\text{HF}$) only, with no change in oxidation states
D) Xenon oxytetrafluoride ($\text{XeOF}_4$), difluorine ($\text{F}_2$), and hydrogen peroxide ($\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$)
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Review the complete hydrolysis equation of $\text{XeF}_4$ given in NCERT Chemistry Class 12:
$6\text{XeF}_4 + 12\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{Xe} + 2\text{XeO}_3 + 24\text{HF} + 3\text{O}_2$.
Step 2: Identify the oxidation states involved in this transformation:
- Xenon in $\text{XeF}_4$ is in the $+4$ oxidation state.
- In the products, xenon disproportionates into elemental $\text{Xe}$ (oxidation state $0$, reduced) and xenon trioxide ($\text{XeO}_3$, where xenon is in $+6$, oxidized).
- Concurrently, oxygen in water (oxidation state $-2$) is oxidized to molecular dioxygen ($\text{O}_2$, oxidation state $0$).
Step 3: Fluorine remains in the $-1$ oxidation state in $\text{HF}$.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: $\text{XeO}_2$ does not form under these conditions; simple non-redox hydrolysis yielding only $\text{XeO}_3$ occurs with $\text{XeF}_6$ ($+\text{6} \rightarrow +\text{6}$), not $\text{XeF}_4$; and no $\text{F}_2$ gas or $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ is liberated.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding the partial and complete hydrolysis of xenon hexafluoride ($\text{XeF}_6$):
Statement I: Partial hydrolysis of $\text{XeF}_6$ with one equivalent of water yields a colourless volatile liquid, xenon oxytetrafluoride ($\text{XeOF}_4$).
Statement II: Partial hydrolysis of $\text{XeF}_6$ with two equivalents of water produces xenon dioxydifluoride ($\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$), whereas complete hydrolysis with three equivalents of water yields an explosive solid, xenon trioxide ($\text{XeO}_3$).
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Statement I: The partial hydrolysis of $\text{XeF}_6$ with equimolar water proceeds as:
$\text{XeF}_6 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{XeOF}_4 + 2\text{HF}$.
$\text{XeOF}_4$ is a colourless volatile liquid with a square pyramidal shape. Thus, Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Analyze Statement II: Further partial hydrolysis with two equivalents of water proceeds as:
$\text{XeF}_6 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2 + 4\text{HF}$.
Upon complete hydrolysis with three equivalents of water:
$\text{XeF}_6 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{XeO}_3 + 6\text{HF}$.
$\text{XeO}_3$ is a colourless, hygroscopic, and violently explosive solid. Thus, Statement II is correct.
Step 3: Both statements precisely match the stepwise hydrolysis reactions documented in NCERT Chemistry Class 12.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Since all stoichiometric products, physical states, and reaction steps are exact, any option alleging either statement to be incorrect is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Xenon fluorides participate in fluoride ion transfer reactions by behaving either as fluoride ion donors or fluoride ion acceptors. What products $\text{P}_1$ and $\text{P}_2$ are formed in the following two chemical transformations?
Reaction 1: $\text{XeF}_2 + \text{PF}_5 \rightarrow \text{P}_1$
Reaction 2: $\text{XeF}_6 + \text{CsF} \rightarrow \text{P}_2$
options: A) $\text{P}_1 = \text{Xe} + \text{PF}_7$ and $\text{P}_2 = \text{Cs}[\text{XeF}_5] + \text{F}_2$
B) $\text{P}_1 = [\text{XeF}_3]^+[\text{PF}_4]^-$ and $\text{P}_2 = [\text{CsF}_2]^-[\text{XeF}_5]^+$
C) $\text{P}_1 = [\text{XeF}]^+[\text{PF}_6]^-$ and $\text{P}_2 = \text{Cs}^+[\text{XeF}_7]^-$
D) $\text{P}_1 = [\text{Xe}]^{2+}[\text{PF}_7]^{2-}$ and $\text{P}_2 = \text{Cs}^+[\text{XeF}_5]^- + \text{F}_2$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Reaction 1: Xenon fluorides react with strong fluoride ion acceptors (Lewis acids like $\text{PF}_5$, $\text{SbF}_5$, $\text{AsF}_5$) to form cationic xenon species by donating a fluoride ion:
$\text{XeF}_2 + \text{PF}_5 \rightarrow [\text{XeF}]^+[\text{PF}_6]^-$.
Here, $\text{XeF}_2$ acts as a fluoride donor.
Step 2: Analyze Reaction 2: With alkali metal fluorides ($\text{MF}$, where $\text{M} = \text{Na}, \text{K}, \text{Rb}, \text{Cs}$), which act as fluoride donors, $\text{XeF}_6$ accepts a fluoride ion to form fluoroanions:
$\text{XeF}_6 + \text{CsF} \rightarrow \text{Cs}^+[\text{XeF}_7]^-$.
Here, $\text{XeF}_6$ acts as a fluoride acceptor.
Step 3: Combining both reactions, $\text{P}_1 = [\text{XeF}]^+[\text{PF}_6]^-$ and $\text{P}_2 = \text{Cs}^+[\text{XeF}_7]^-$.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Species such as $\text{PF}_7$ do not exist; phosphorus cannot expand its valence shell to 14 electrons; and fluoride transfer does not liberate elemental $\text{F}_2$ gas.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Certain metallic elements such as aluminium ($\text{Al}$) and chromium ($\text{Cr}$) do not dissolve in concentrated nitric acid and become chemically passive.
Reason (R): Concentrated nitric acid is a powerful oxidizing agent that forms an impervious, unreactive microscopic passive oxide film on the metal surface that protects the bulk metal from further chemical attack.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: A) (A) is false but (R) is true
B) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
C) (A) is true but (R) is false
D) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Assertion (A): When reactive metals like $\text{Al}$, $\text{Cr}$, and $\text{Fe}$ are immersed in concentrated nitric acid ($>68\%$), they quickly cease to react and become completely passive to subsequent acid exposure. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.
Step 2: Analyze Reason (R): Concentrated nitric acid is an exceptionally potent oxidizing agent. Upon contact with the clean metal surface, it immediately oxidizes the metal atoms to form an extremely thin, coherent, and non-porous layer of metal oxide (such as $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ or $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$). This protective oxide film acts as a mechanical barrier preventing direct contact between hydrogen ions and the underlying metal. Thus, Reason (R) is true.
Step 3: Reason (R) provides the definitive physicochemical explanation for the phenomenon of metal passivity asserted in (A). Hence, both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Options asserting that (A) or (R) is false are inconsistent with standard NCERT metallurgy and p-block principles regarding the action of oxidizing acids.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Match List I (Xenon Compound) with List II (VSEPR Geometry & Hybridization):
List I:
A. $\text{XeF}_2$
B. $\text{XeOF}_4$
C. $\text{XeF}_6$
D. $\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$

List II:
1. Distorted octahedral ($sp^3d^3$, 6 bond pairs + 1 lone pair)
2. Linear ($sp^3d$, 2 bond pairs + 3 equatorial lone pairs)
3. See-saw ($sp^3d$, 4 bond pairs + 1 equatorial lone pair)
4. Square pyramidal ($sp^3d^2$, 5 bond pairs + 1 lone pair)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Match A: $\text{XeF}_2$ has 2 bonding pairs and 3 lone pairs (steric number 5, $sp^3d$ hybridization). The three lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, giving a linear geometry. Hence, A matches with 2.
Step 2: Match B: $\text{XeOF}_4$ has 1 double-bonded oxygen and 4 single-bonded fluorines (5 bonding directions) plus 1 lone pair (steric number 6, $sp^3d^2$ hybridization). This produces a square pyramidal geometry. Hence, B matches with 4.
Step 3: Match C: $\text{XeF}_6$ has 6 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair (steric number 7, $sp^3d^3$ hybridization). The lone pair causes distortion, resulting in a distorted octahedral geometry. Hence, C matches with 1.
Step 4: Match D: $\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$ has 2 double-bonded oxygens, 2 single-bonded fluorines, and 1 lone pair (steric number 5, $sp^3d$ hybridization). The lone pair occupies an equatorial position, yielding a see-saw geometry. Hence, D matches with 3. Therefore, the correct matching is A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding the allotropic forms of sulfur:
Statement I: Both rhombic sulfur ($\alpha$-sulfur) and monoclinic sulfur ($\beta$-sulfur) are composed of puckered cyclic $\text{S}_8$ rings adopting a crown conformation with an $\text{S}-\text{S}-\text{S}$ bond angle of approximately $107^\circ$.
Statement II: In Engel's sulfur ($\text{S}_6$ allotrope), the sulfur atoms form a completely planar hexagonal ring with an $\text{S}-\text{S}-\text{S}$ bond angle of exactly $120^\circ$.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
B) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
C) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
D) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Statement I: Rhombic ($\alpha$) and monoclinic ($\beta$) sulfur differ only in the packing and symmetry of the crystalline lattice. Both allotropes consist of identical eight-membered puckered crown-shaped $\text{S}_8$ rings where the $\text{S}-\text{S}$ bond length is $204\text{ pm}$ and the $\text{S}-\text{S}-\text{S}$ bond angle is $107^\circ$. Thus, Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Analyze Statement II: Synthesized forms of sulfur containing smaller rings, such as $\text{S}_6$ (Engel's sulfur), do not adopt a planar geometry. To avoid severe angle strain and eclipsing lone-pair interactions, the $\text{S}_6$ ring adopts a puckered chair conformation with an $\text{S}-\text{S}-\text{S}$ bond angle of $102.2^\circ$ and an $\text{S}-\text{S}$ bond length of $205.7\text{ pm}$. Thus, Statement II is incorrect.
Step 3: Consequently, Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Stating that both are correct overlooks the non-planar chair conformation of the six-membered sulfur ring.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): In aqueous solution, sulfuric acid ionizes in two sequential stages where the first ionization constant is very large ($K_{a_1} > 10$), while the second ionization constant is significantly smaller ($K_{a_2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}$ at $298\text{ K}$).
Reason (R): It is electrostatic work to remove a positively charged proton ($\text{H}^+$) from a negatively charged hydrogen sulfate ion ($[\text{HSO}_4]^-$) compared to removing it from a neutral $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ molecule.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: A) (A) is true but (R) is false
B) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
C) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
D) (A) is false but (R) is true
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Assertion (A): In water, sulfuric acid dissociates according to:
$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{HSO}_4^- \quad (K_{a_1} > 10)$
$\text{HSO}_4^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{SO}_4^{2-} \quad (K_{a_2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2})$.
Because $K_{a_1}$ is very large, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acts as a strong electrolyte in the first dissociation step. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.
Step 2: Analyze Reason (R): In the first step, a proton is detached from an electrically neutral $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ molecule. In the second step, the proton must be pulled away against the strong electrostatic attraction of the negatively charged monovalent anion $[\text{HSO}_4]^-$. This requires substantially more energy, shifting the equilibrium toward the left and causing $K_{a_2} \ll K_{a_1}$. Thus, Reason (R) is true.
Step 3: Reason (R) correctly provides the fundamental electrostatic basis for the observed disparity between $K_{a_1}$ and $K_{a_2}$. Hence, both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Any choice claiming (A) or (R) is false or non-explanatory contradicts the classical principles of polyprotic acid ionization.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding the comparative chemistry of nitrogen and heavier Group 15 elements:
I. Nitrogen has a unique ability to form $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds with itself and with other elements having small size and high electronegativity (such as $\text{C}$ and $\text{O}$).
II. Heavier congeners (such as phosphorus and arsenic) do not readily form $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds because their atomic orbitals are too large and diffuse to undergo effective lateral overlap.
III. The single $\text{N}-\text{N}$ bond is considerably weaker than the single $\text{P}-\text{P}$ bond because of high interelectronic repulsion between non-bonding lone pairs on the small nitrogen atoms.
IV. Consequently, the tendency for catenation is significantly weaker in nitrogen than in phosphorus.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: A) I, II, III, and IV
B) II, III, and IV only
C) I and IV only
D) I, II, and III only
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Statement I: Nitrogen's small atomic radius enables effective lateral overlap of $2p$ orbitals, forming stable triple bonds ($\text{N} \equiv \text{N}$), as well as multiple bonds with carbon ($\text{C} \equiv \text{N}$) and oxygen ($\text{N}=\text{O}$). (Statement I is correct).
Step 2: Statement II: The $3p$ orbitals of phosphorus and $4p$ of arsenic are larger and more diffuse; lateral overlap is inefficient, so heavier elements prefer forming single $\sigma$-bonds instead of $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds. (Statement II is correct).
Step 3: Statement III: The $\text{N}-\text{N}$ single bond dissociation enthalpy ($160\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) is much lower than the $\text{P}-\text{P}$ single bond enthalpy ($213\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) due to severe electrostatic repulsion between the non-bonding electron pairs concentrated on the adjacent compact nitrogen atoms. (Statement III is correct).
Step 4: Statement IV: Catenation requires strong homoatomic single bonds. Because the single $\text{N}-\text{N}$ bond is weak, nitrogen shows very limited catenation (rarely exceeding 3 atoms as in azides, $\text{N}_3^-$), whereas phosphorus forms extended chains and rings. (Statement IV is correct). Thus, all statements I, II, III, and IV are correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Concentrated sulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) acts as a moderately strong oxidizing agent when heated with non-metals such as elemental carbon and sulfur. What are the total moles of gaseous products evolved when $1\text{ mole}$ of carbon and $1\text{ mole}$ of sulfur are separately oxidized completely by an excess of hot concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$?
options: A) $1\text{ mole}$ of gas from carbon oxidation, and $2\text{ moles}$ of gas from sulfur oxidation
B) $3\text{ moles}$ of gas from carbon oxidation, and $3\text{ moles}$ of gas from sulfur oxidation
C) $2\text{ moles}$ of gas from carbon oxidation, and $1\text{ mole}$ of gas from sulfur oxidation
D) $4\text{ moles}$ of gas from carbon oxidation, and $6\text{ moles}$ of gas from sulfur oxidation
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Write the balanced redox reaction for the oxidation of carbon by hot concentrated sulfuric acid:
$\text{C} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{ (conc.)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{SO}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$.
From $1\text{ mole}$ of carbon, the gaseous products are $1\text{ mole of } \text{CO}_2$ and $2\text{ moles of } \text{SO}_2$, yielding a total of $1 + 2 = 3\text{ moles}$ of gas.
Step 2: Write the balanced redox reaction for the oxidation of sulfur by hot concentrated sulfuric acid:
$\text{S} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{ (conc.)} \rightarrow 3\text{SO}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$.
From $1\text{ mole}$ of sulfur, the gaseous product is $3\text{ moles of } \text{SO}_2$.
Step 3: Therefore, both reactions yield exactly $3\text{ moles}$ of gaseous products per mole of non-metal oxidized.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: Overlooking either $\text{CO}_2$ or the stoichiometric coefficient of $\text{SO}_2$ leads to incorrect gaseous totals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The large-scale industrial manufacture of nitric acid ($\text{HNO}_3$) via Ostwald's process involves three sequential chemical steps. Which of the following analytical summaries accurately describes the reaction conditions, catalyst, and chemical principles governing these steps?
options: A) Step 1: Oxidation of dinitrogen ($\text{N}_2$) and dihydrogen ($\text{H}_2$) to $\text{NO}_2$ in an electric arc furnace; Step 2: Catalytic hydrogenation; Step 3: Absorption in dilute sulfuric acid

B) Step 1: Direct catalytic oxidation of $\text{NH}_3$ to $\text{HNO}_3$ over vanadium pentoxide ($\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$) at $1000\text{ K}$; Step 2: Condensation of acid mist; Step 3: Dehydration with $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$

C) Step 1: Catalytic oxidation of $\text{NH}_3$ by air over $\text{Pt}/\text{Rh}$ gauze catalyst at $500\text{ K}$ and $9\text{ bar}$ to form $\text{NO}$; Step 2: Oxidation of $\text{NO}$ to $\text{NO}_2$; Step 3: Dissolution of $\text{NO}_2$ in water to yield $\text{HNO}_3$ and recyclable $\text{NO}$

D) Step 1: Thermal cracking of $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$ to yield $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$; Step 2: Catalytic reduction of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$ over iron gauze; Step 3: Hydration to yield $98\%$ nitric acid
questions.explanation:
Step 1: In Ostwald's process, Step 1 is the catalytic oxidation of ammonia by atmospheric oxygen:
$4\text{NH}_3(\text{g}) + 5\text{O}_2(\text{g}) \xrightarrow{\text{Pt}/\text{Rh gauge, } 500\text{ K, } 9\text{ bar}} 4\text{NO}(\text{g}) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{g})$.
This exothermic reaction achieves high conversion yields rapidly over the platinum-rhodium catalyst.
Step 2: In Step 2, the generated nitric oxide is cooled and combined with dioxygen to yield nitrogen dioxide:
$2\text{NO}(\text{g}) + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(\text{g})$.
Step 3: In Step 3, nitrogen dioxide dissolves in water to form nitric acid, regenerating nitric oxide which is recycled back into Step 2:
$3\text{NO}_2(\text{g}) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) \rightarrow 2\text{HNO}_3(\text{aq}) + \text{NO}(\text{g})$.
Aqueous $\text{HNO}_3$ obtained can be concentrated by distillation up to $\approx 68\%$, and further concentrated to $98\%$ by dehydration with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
Step 4: Distractor analysis: $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ is used in the Contact process, not Ostwald's process; the electric arc process is the obsolete Birkeland-Eyde process; and ammonium nitrate cracking does not form $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding the molecular electronic structures and magnetic properties of nitrogen oxides:
I. In gaseous nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$), the unpaired electron resides in an antibonding $\pi^*_{2p}$ molecular orbital, giving a bond order of $2.5$.
II.
